title: Design Skiplist
description: Brute force to optimized: a sorted array with binary search versus a true multi-level randomized skiplist achieving O(log n) for all operations.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Design a Skiplist without using any built-in libraries, supporting search(target) (return whether target exists), add(num) (insert num), and erase(num) (remove one occurrence of num if present, returning whether it was removed).

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Skiplist\" explicitly named, without built-in libraries","A multi-level linked list structure, where higher levels skip over more elements, giving BST-like O(log n) average performance"],["Search, insert, delete all needed efficiently","Each level acts as an \"express lane,\" letting search drop down a level whenever it would overshoot"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

A skiplist maintains multiple linked layers of increasing sparsity: the bottom layer holds all elements in sorted order, and each layer above skips over roughly half the elements of the layer below (typically via random coin-flips deciding a new element's height). Searching starts at the topmost, sparsest layer and drops down whenever the next node would overshoot the target, giving expected O(log n) performance without needing tree rotations.

blocks.title: Analogy: An Express Train System with Progressively Fewer Stops
blocks.text: Picture a train system where the express line stops at very few stations, a semi-express line stops at more, and the local line stops everywhere. To reach a specific station, you ride the express line as far as possible, switch down a level when it would overshoot your destination, and repeat, reaching any station in relatively few total stops.

blocks.caption: Multiple express-lane levels; search drops a level whenever the next node would overshoot the target

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: add(1), add(2), add(3), search(0), add(4), search(1), erase(0), erase(1), search(1)
Results: null, null, null, false, null, true, false, true, false. search(0) is false (0 was never added); erase(1) succeeds and removes it, so the final search(1) is false.
5. How Should We Think?

Before using a single flat sorted structure (which needs O(n) shifting for insert/erase), notice that a true skiplist uses MULTIPLE linked layers of decreasing density, letting search, insert, and erase all achieve expected O(log n) by navigating level by level, similar in spirit to a balanced BST but built from linked lists instead of tree rotations.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The bottom level of a skiplist is simply a sorted linked list containing every element.

Observation 2: Each level above skips over roughly half the nodes of the level below it, typically decided by a random "coin flip" for each newly inserted element's height, giving expected logarithmic depth.

Observation 3: A search starts at the topmost, sparsest level, moving forward as long as the next node's value does not exceed the target, and drops down a level whenever it would overshoot, continuing until the bottom level is reached.

Observation 4: Insertion and deletion follow the same level-by-level navigation to find the correct position(s) at each level, updating pointers directly rather than shifting elements, unlike an array-based structure.

This leads to a multi-level linked list structure, where each level acts as an express lane over the level below, giving expected O(log n) for search, add, and erase, all without any array shifting or tree rotations.
6. Brute Force Solution
Maintain a single sorted array. Use binary search for search(), but insertion and removal require shifting elements.
Why the code is written this way

items: A sorted array directly supports O(log n) search via binary search.
Insertion and removal require shifting subsequent elements, costing O(n) each, missing the intended average O(log n) for ALL operations.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(log n) for search, O(n) for add and erase (due to shifting).
Space: O(n).
Limitation: a true multi-level skiplist structure achieves expected O(log n) for ALL THREE operations, avoiding any array shifting.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Build a genuine multi-level linked structure: the bottom level holds all elements in sorted order via next pointers; each higher level "expresses" over roughly half the nodes of the level below, with each node's height decided randomly at insertion time (e.g., repeated coin flips). Searching drops down a level whenever advancing would overshoot the target, giving expected O(log n) traversal. Insertion and deletion locate the correct position at every relevant level using this same search, then splice in or remove the node's pointers directly at each level, an O(1) pointer update per level rather than an O(n) shift.

Maintain multiple linked levels with randomized node heights. search/add/erase all navigate level by level (dropping down on overshoot), updating pointers directly rather than shifting array elements.
9. Optimized Solution
Conceptual structure (simplified)

blocks.caption: A true multi-level skiplist gives O(log n) average for all operations via level-by-level pointer updates

blocks.text: Why This Works

Randomizing each node's height so that roughly half of level i's nodes also appear in level i+1 gives an EXPECTED logarithmic number of levels, and searching by starting at the top and dropping down on overshoot visits an expected O(log n) nodes total. Since insertion and deletion only ever update pointers directly (never shifting array elements), both also achieve expected O(log n), matching balanced-BST-like performance without needing explicit tree rotations.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(log n) expected for search, add, and erase.
Space: O(n) expected total (each node has O(1) expected levels).

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Design Skiplist is a foundational exercise in implementing a probabilistic alternative to balanced BSTs, achieving similar expected performance through randomized layering instead of deterministic rotations.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting to update the "update" pointer array at EVERY relevant level during insertion or deletion, corrupting the multi-level structure.
Not handling the case where the skiplist's overall level needs to increase due to a newly inserted, taller node.

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Explicitly explaining the probabilistic height assignment and WHY it gives expected O(log n) levels demonstrates genuine understanding of skiplists, not just a memorized structure.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "design a probabilistic alternative to a balanced BST", think: a multi-level linked structure with randomized node heights, dropping down a level on overshoot.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you make this structure support duplicate ranks/counts efficiently?
How does a skiplist's expected performance compare to a balanced BST's worst-case guarantees?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Any "probabilistic balanced structure" design problem, using randomization instead of deterministic rebalancing.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The sorted-array approach costs O(log n) for search but O(n) for add/erase; a true multi-level skiplist costs O(log n) expected for all three operations, using O(n) expected space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: a multi-level linked structure with randomized node heights, a probabilistic alternative to balanced BSTs.
Core Idea: search drops down a level whenever advancing would overshoot the target; add/erase update pointers directly at every relevant level.
Time: O(log n) search but O(n) add/erase for a sorted array, O(log n) expected for all three in a true skiplist.
Most Important Observation: randomized node heights give expected logarithmic levels, achieving BST-like performance without rotations.
Interview Difficulty: a genuinely hard design problem, testing understanding of probabilistic data structures.
One line memory trick: multiple linked levels, randomized heights, drop down on overshoot.
